paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas C. Early took place in Leadville, Colorado, on March 28, 1882, after Early, a local lawyer and politician, shot and killed police officer Samuel Townsend. Wire reports said an attempt to lynch Early was frustrated, and a Missouri paper reported that he was kept under strong guard at the jail against a mob that threatened to lynch him. An inquest jury recommended that Early be held for the grand jury without bail.

Early, aged about 27 or 28 and a native of the south, had practiced law in Leadville for about three years after living in Sedalia, Missouri, where he had been a reporter and a school principal. Townsend, about forty, was a Leadville police officer and the constable of Judge Talbot's court, and had earlier served as a deputy sheriff. Their dispute arose from a replevin suit brought by Mamie Mordell against Carrie Adams, in which Early, as Mordell's counsel, claimed that Townsend had overcharged him ten or fifteen cents in fees.

Shortly before 3 p.m., passers-by on Harrison Avenue near Fifth Street heard three pistol shots from the hallway of the Union block and found Townsend lying on the landing with a wound in the abdomen. According to the Leadville account, Early fired with deliberate aim and Townsend's gun was still in its sheath, while the Rutland Herald said the fatal shot went off as Townsend tried to wrench the pistol away. Townsend died within about half an hour.

Detective John Byrne arrested Early at the scene and took him into a hat store next door as a dense crowd filled the street. The Sedalia Weekly Bazoo reported that Early was then hurried to jail and placed under a strong guard to protect him from a mob that had gathered and threatened to lynch him. The same paper said that friends of the dead officer "would surely have resorted to violence if permitted," but no account describes what the crowd did.

Early claimed self-defense, but eyewitnesses quoted by the Rutland Herald said Townsend had neither struck him nor tried to shoot. A Denver Republican dispatch reported that the inquest jury found the shooting "deliberate and unprovoked," recommended that Early be held without bail, and described feeling against him as very bitter. No report of a grand jury indictment or a trial was found in the coverage.

The story spread through a Denver News dispatch from Leadville, which ran on March 29 and 30 in papers from St. Paul to Salt Lake City and Nevada under headings such as "A Murderous Attorney" and "From Politics to the Gallows." In these briefs the lynching attempt was a single closing sentence, and condensed versions in the Maysville Evening Bulletin, the Bismarck Tribune and weekly crime columns kept it while some shorter briefs dropped it.

The fullest coverage came from Sedalia, where the Weekly Bazoo treated Early as a former townsman, headlining that he had been "Rescued With Difficulty From a Mob" and reprinting a long Leadville account titled "Cold Blood Murder." A Vermont paper, reprinting the Rutland Herald, covered the killing as an obituary of Townsend, a Vermont native, and did not mention the mob. No paper identified either man by race.

Reports differed on the time and day of the shooting: the wire said "this evening," the Leadville account said shortly before 3 o'clock, and the Bazoo brief said Monday. The wire gave the lawyer's name as J. C. Early, while the Sedalia paper, which knew him, and the Leadville account called him Thomas C. Early.

bases: Wire reports say an attempt to lynch Early, who had just shot a policeman, was frustrated (A1, A5), and a Sedalia report says a mob gathered and threatened to lynch him while he was jailed under guard (A9); no one was killed by the crowd.

A mob threatened or attempted to lynch Early for the shooting of Townsend, but officers kept him under guard and he was not harmed (A1, A9); with no one killed, the episode does not meet the standard definition.

The wire report of a frustrated lynching attempt (A1, A5) and the separately written Sedalia report of a mob threatening to lynch him at the jail (A9) agree on the core event, though neither describes the crowd's actions in detail.

framing.detail: Wire briefs ran the shooting with the lynching attempt as a final sentence, under heads such as 'A Murderous Attorney' and 'Police Officer Killed'.
The Sedalia Bazoo, writing of a former townsman, headlined that he was 'Rescued With Difficulty From a Mob' and reported the mob threat without comment on it.
The reprinted Leadville account, 'Cold Blood Murder', condemned Early's act in strong language but did not mention the mob in the portion printed.
